newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French debt finished a second rough day in a row lower with PIBOR interest rate futures succumbing again to franc weakness as non-residents sold amid fears of labour unrest, traders said.
Many economists said a crisis was not on the cards but some acknowledged that there was little reason to buy francs or that the currency was somewhat vulnerable in the very short term.

The franc was trading at 3.4260/65 against the mark at 1451 GMT compared to 3.4202/05 in late afternoon European trading on Tuesday and 3.4077/80 last Thursday after the Bundesbank and the Bank of France cut interest rates.
PIBOR, which had closed 13 basis points lower at 95.86 on Tuesday as the franc lingered below 3.42 against the mark, settled another 10 basis points down on Wednesday at 95.76.
The 10-year future, which had also shed 16 basis points on Tuesday, lost a further 16 on Wednesday to finish at 122.96, off its day lows but below the key 123 support level.
One trader said investors awaiting a number of bond issues in the pipeline were looking for the market to come a bit lower.
Worries about unions stirring up labour unrest and protest against the 1997 budget are overdone, many economists say.

Louis Viannet, head of Communist-led CGT union blamed the government spending cut drive and the "forced march" to monetary union for economic gloom and high unemployment in a news conference on Wednesday but stopped short of calling a strike for now.
His remarks follow warnings from Socialist CFDT union leader Nicole Notat on Tuesday that there could be conflict.
Teachers unions are also considering a possible strike over education cuts and reforms but will meet again on September 3 to decide their course of action.
Force Ouvriere leader Marc Blondel is due to be interviewed on RTL radio at 0550 GMT on Thursday.
The franc, which hit its lowest level since the end of March on August 13 at 3.4280 before bouncing back after German and French rate cuts, hit a low of 3.4171 earlier on Wednesday.

Economists say the Prime Minister Alain Juppe's budget, due to be presented by mid-September, should not be cause for concern, that the political commitment to European monetary is intact and pressure on the franc should be shortlived.

Juppe, who reconvened his cabinet on Wednesday after the summer break, said the government had missed its target on unemployment and should "move up a gear" on the issue. He also said the government would push on with reform.
